steps.title: Student makes a StudentAid.gov account
steps.summary: This account (often called the FSA ID) is how the student signs the FAFSA. Only the student may make and use it.
how: Open StudentAid.gov and choose Create Account.
Use the student's own personal email and cell phone, not a school email that stops working after graduation.
Enter the name, date of birth and Social Security number exactly as they appear on the Social Security card.
Save the username, password and backup code in a password manager or somewhere safe at home.
The Social Security check can take 1 to 3 days. You can start the FAFSA while you wait.
watch_out: Never type the FSA ID, password or Social Security number into ScholarTasks. We will never ask for them.
A parent must not make or use the student's account, even to help. Each person signs with their own.

steps.title: Each contributing parent makes their own account
steps.summary: Every parent who has to take part (see Who fills in the FAFSA below) needs their own StudentAid.gov account to give consent and sign.
how: Check the household questions below first so you know which parent or parents are contributors.
Each contributor opens StudentAid.gov and chooses Create Account, using their own email and phone.
A parent without a Social Security number can still make an account. Choose the option for people without one.
Save the login somewhere safe. You'll use the same account every year your student files.
watch_out: One email and one phone number can belong to only one StudentAid.gov account. Parents can't share the student's.

steps.title: Answer a few questions about your household
steps.summary: Six quick questions tell you which parents must take part and which papers to gather. No numbers, no ID numbers.
how: Answer the household questions on this page. A parent can change them any time.
ScholarTasks then shows who the FAFSA contributors are and builds your document list.

link.label: Official help: who's my FAFSA parent?

steps.title: Gather your documents
steps.summary: Have these ready before you sit down so the FAFSA takes about 20 minutes. Tick each one off as you find it.
how: Use the list on this page. It is built from your household answers.
Most tax numbers move over from the IRS by themselves once each contributor gives consent, so you mostly need the return to check against.
Asset amounts (cash, savings, investments) are as of the day you file, not from the tax year.

steps.title: List the colleges to send the FAFSA to
steps.summary: You can send the FAFSA to up to 20 colleges at once, free. Add every college the student is applying to, even if unsure.
how: Look at the Colleges list on your ScholarTasks plan.
On the FAFSA, search each college by name or by its federal school code.
Add a college you're not sure about. It costs nothing and you can remove it later.
Add each college's own financial aid priority date below so you get reminders.

steps.title: Student starts the {cycle} FAFSA and invites contributors
steps.summary: The student signs in, fills in their own part and invites each contributor by email or with a text code.
how: Student signs in at StudentAid.gov and starts the {cycle} FAFSA (the year you start college).
Answer the student questions and add the colleges.
When asked about parents, invite each contributor. They get an email or a code by text.
Give consent for the IRS to share the student's tax information. If the student didn't file taxes, they still give consent.
Sign and submit the student section.
watch_out: Pick the {cycle} form, not the one for the current school year.
Without consent from every contributor, the FAFSA can't be processed and no aid can be offered.

steps.title: Each contributor fills in their part and signs
steps.summary: Each contributor opens the invitation, signs in with their own account, gives IRS consent, adds what the IRS doesn't know, and signs.
how: Open the invitation email or enter the text code at StudentAid.gov.
Give consent to share your federal tax information. This is required, even if you didn't file.
Check the tax numbers that come over, then enter cash, savings and investment amounts as of today.
Enter the family size and how many are in college.
Sign. The FAFSA is complete only when every contributor has signed.
watch_out: Don't count the home you live in, retirement accounts or life insurance as investments.
If you filed a tax return with a different spouse or an amended return, the IRS may not send numbers. You'll type them in from your return.

steps.title: Check the FAFSA shows as submitted
steps.summary: Make sure everyone signed and the status says Submitted. Save the confirmation email.
how: Student signs in and checks the FAFSA status on the dashboard.
If it says Pending or Action Required, someone still has to sign or give consent.
Save the confirmation email from Federal Student Aid.

steps.title: CSS Profile, only if a college asks for it
steps.summary: Some private colleges use the CSS Profile for their own grant money. Georgia public colleges generally don't. Check each college's financial aid page.
how: Check each college's financial aid page for "CSS Profile" and its due date.
Make a College Board account for the student and fill it in with a parent.
There is a fee for each college, and many families get it waived automatically.
Some colleges also ask the other parent (in divorced families) to fill in a part.
watch_out: Mark this step Doesn't apply if none of your colleges ask for it.

steps.title: Read your FAFSA Submission Summary
steps.summary: A few days after you submit, the summary shows your Student Aid Index (SAI) and an estimate of Pell Grant eligibility. Check it for mistakes.
how: Student signs in to StudentAid.gov and opens the FAFSA Submission Summary.
Check names, dates of birth, the college list and the money numbers.
If something is wrong, make a correction. Corrections are open until {corrections}.
The SAI is not what you'll pay. Each college uses it to work out your aid.

steps.title: Check each college's aid portal for a to-do list
steps.summary: After you apply, each college gives you a student portal. Their financial aid page may ask for more forms or documents.
how: Open each college's applicant portal from your admissions email.
Look for a financial aid section, to-do list or "missing documents".
Do any to-do items quickly. Aid offers wait until they're done.
Check again every couple of weeks until you have an offer.

steps.title: Send verification documents if asked
steps.summary: Some FAFSAs are picked for verification, a check of the numbers. It's routine. The college tells you what to send.
how: Watch email and each college portal for a verification request.
Send exactly what the college lists, through their secure portal, by their date.
Ask the college's aid office if anything is unclear. Never email tax papers to anyone else.
watch_out: Mark this step Doesn't apply if no college has asked.

steps.title: Compare aid offers side by side
steps.summary: Compare what each college would really cost after grants and scholarships. Loans are money you pay back, so don't count them as aid.
how: For each offer, find the full cost of attendance (tuition, housing, food, books, travel).
Subtract grants and scholarships only (free money, including HOPE or Zell).
What's left is your real cost, to cover with savings, work, or loans.
Check whether each scholarship renews every year and what GPA it needs.

steps.title: Ask for a review if your situation changed
steps.summary: If your income dropped, a job was lost, or there are big medical bills, the FAFSA's tax-year numbers may be out of date. Colleges can adjust.
how: Contact each college's financial aid office and ask for a "special circumstances" or "professional judgment" review.
Explain the change in a short letter and attach proof (for example a layoff letter).
Ask politely; a college may also match a better offer from a similar college.
watch_out: Mark this step Doesn't apply if nothing changed.

steps.title: Accept the aid at your chosen college
steps.summary: Accept grants and scholarships in the college's portal. If you borrow, there are two short online steps first.
how: Accept the grants and scholarships in the chosen college's portal by their deadline.
Tell the college about any outside scholarships you've won.
If borrowing federal loans, do Entrance Counseling and sign the Master Promissory Note at StudentAid.gov.
Borrow only what you need. You can turn down or lower a loan.

steps.title: Remember to file again every year
steps.summary: The FAFSA must be filed every year of college. It usually opens October 1 for the next year, and later years can copy some answers.
how: Add a reminder for October of your student's first college year.
Use the same StudentAid.gov accounts. Don't make new ones.

documents.text: Student's Social Security number (keep it handy, don't type it here)
Each contributor's own StudentAid.gov username and password
Parents' {tax_year} federal tax return (Form 1040 and schedules)
documents.hint: Most numbers come over from the IRS. Keep the return open to check them.

documents.text: Parents' {tax_year} W-2s or other records of money earned
documents.hint: For parents who didn't file a {tax_year} return.

documents.text: File the {tax_year} tax return first, or have the income numbers ready
documents.hint: The FAFSA asks about {tax_year}. Most {tax_year} returns are already filed; if yours isn't, the IRS transfer won't work yet.

documents.text: Student's {tax_year} W-2s, or their tax return if they filed one
Current balances of checking and savings accounts and cash on hand
documents.hint: As of the day you file.

documents.text: Current value of investments (brokerage accounts, 529 plans, CDs, real estate other than your home)
documents.hint: Don't include the home you live in or retirement accounts like 401(k)s and IRAs.

documents.text: Net worth of the family business or farm (what it's worth minus what's owed)
documents.hint: Family farms and small businesses now count on the FAFSA.

documents.text: Address and identity details for the parent without a Social Security number
documents.hint: They can still make an account and sign; the IRS transfer may not work, so have income records ready.

documents.text: The list of colleges (up to 20) to send it to

never_store: Tax returns, W-2s or bank statements
